newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian bonds need wages to work on rally.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian bonds need wages to work on rally.

text.p: *Australian bond yields dipped briefly on today's benign inflation outcome, but quickly ran into profit-taking as the market awaited the crucial quarterly wages report on Thursday.
*However, market still outperforms U.S. on the day.

A fall in Australia's inflation rate to a two year low failed to cause too much excitement in the bond market as it continued to look ahead to Thursday's now crucial wages data, and yields ended slightly higher.

Analysts said if not for last week's wages-cautious RBA Bulletin, the market would have been screaming for a cut in interest rates on today's inflation outcome, which saw the policy sensitive underlying rate back within the RBA's target.
Instead bonds drew profit-taking with yields having eased a 1/4 point since Thursday in anticipation of the data result.

"The first leg of the double needed for the Reserve Bank to decide on another rate cut at the Melbourne Cup day board meeting fell into place today," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.
However, he added that only if average weekly ordinary time earnings for the August quarter rise of 0.9 percent, or lower, would a November rate cut become a "red hot favourite".
The headline CPI rose 0.3 percent in the September quarter for an annual rate of 2.1 percent, while underlying inflation rose 0.5 percent to a year-on-year rate of 2.4 percent.
Both annual rates were 3.1 percent in the June quarter.
Median expectations for AWOTE centre on a 1.0 percent rise which would bring the annual rate to 3.7 percent.
However, some economists believe the RBA will want to see even more data than just today's data and AWOTE.

"Our guess is that the enterprise agreements and capex (capital expenditure) reports due at the end of November now hold the key to a further easing in monetary policy," said Andrew Pease, senior economist at Nomura Research Australia.
Wages growth in enterprise bargaining agreements and business investment were two key areas the central bank highlighted in its quarterly economic review.

Local bonds still outperformed the U.S. on the day, despite the small retracement, although the Australian/U.S. 10-year bond yield spread ended above the low 90s seen in early trading. The largest move on the day was against New Zealand, which finally buckled on profit-taking after its recent heady advance.

The December 10-year bond contract touched its highest dayside level in over 2-1/2 years at 92.530 on the data, but short of the afterhours peak of 92.560 seen earlier this month. This high is still achievable if AWOTE proves weak.
